taxes_invoicing.title: Selling 6 — Taxes, Pricing Rules & Invoicing
taxes_invoicing.desc: VAT done right, inclusive vs exclusive, item tax overrides, pricing rules and discounts, the Sales Invoice, payments, credit notes — and the reports that watch it all.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — VAT in Nigeria & the tax architecture
lessons.html:
Every naira of VAT you charge is money you are holding for the government. That single sentence reframes tax from paperwork into fiduciary machinery, and this chapter builds the machinery view a consultant needs before touching a single template.

Output VAT, in one paragraph. Nigerian VAT stands at 7.5%. When you sell taxable goods, you charge it ON TOP of your price (or embedded within it — Chapter 4); the amount is output VAT, and it is not revenue. It accrues into a VAT liability account, and each month the firm files and remits to FIRS — returns due by the 21st of the following month — netting output VAT collected against input VAT paid on purchases. Your firm is a collection agent with a deadline; the system's job is to make the collected number exact, automatic, and auditable.

The architecture principle: write once, apply everywhere. ZhiftERP encodes tax as a Sales Taxes and Charges Template — the policy object — selected on documents, never re-invented on them. One template row says: VAT, 7.5%, posting to the VAT output account. Every quotation, order and invoice that selects the template computes identically, and the liability account accumulates the truth as a by-product of trading. The rejected alternatives define the principle by contrast: VAT typed into item rates hides tax inside price (misstating both, unremittable as a number); VAT computed per document by hand varies with the human; VAT inferred from customer group confuses who is buying with what is taxable.

The account head. The template row names the ledger account the tax posts to — the VAT output liability in your chart. This is the joint where selling meets accounting: at month-end, the filing figure is READ from that account, and Chapter 9 shows the reconciliation that proves it against the invoice register. A template pointed at the wrong account (an income account, a random liability) files fiction with a straight face; verify the head once at setup and the joint holds forever.

Who decides what. Configuration is a consultant-plus-accountant conversation: the accountant owns which accounts and what the firm's filing posture is; the consultant owns encoding it so the sales floor never has to know. The seller's entire tax job, done right, is selecting the correct template — and Chapters 2-4 make even that mostly automatic.

The NGE thread. Where regulatory e-invoicing applies — the FIRS pipeline your NGE Portal serves — the invoice data transmitted downstream is only as clean as this architecture: the VAT the platform reports IS the template-computed figure on template-driven documents. A firm whose tax lives in templates passes e-invoicing validation as a by-product; a firm whose tax lives in typed rates and habits meets the mandate as a re-implementation project. Architecture first is also compliance first.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Building Sales Taxes and Charges Templates
lessons.html:
The template is a small machine: ordered rows, each computing a charge and posting it somewhere. Build one deliberately once and you will read every tax section in the system fluently forever.

Row anatomy. Each row carries: a Type — the computation base; the Account Head — where it posts; the Rate (or amount); and a description that prints. The types to command:

  • On Net Total — the workhorse: percentage of the document's net (pre-tax) total. Nigerian VAT is one row, On Net Total, 7.5%, VAT output account.
  • Actual — a fixed amount regardless of totals: a ₦15,000 delivery charge as a line the customer sees, posting to a freight-recovery account.
  • On Previous Row Amount / Total — compounding bases for cascading levies; rare in plain Nigerian trade but the reading knowledge matters — when you meet a template using them, the ORDER of rows is part of the arithmetic.

Charges are rows too. The same machinery carries non-tax charges — delivery fees, installation surcharges — each with its own account head. A document then presents goods, charges, and VAT as distinct lines summing to one grand total (Selling 3, Chapter 4 made the customer-facing case). Discipline: charges post to their own recovery accounts, never mingled into the VAT head — the filing figure must stay pure.

How many templates. Few. A standard-rated template (VAT 7.5%); perhaps a with-delivery variant; a zero-VAT template for the export/exempt document cases Chapter 3 does not cover row-wise. Template sprawl — one per customer, one per month — is policy chaos: when the rate changes or an account is remapped, every template is a separate edit and a separate chance to miss one. Encode DIFFERENCES that are item-level as Item Tax Templates (Chapter 3), not as document-template proliferation.

Defaulting. Mark the standard template as default and it lands on new documents automatically; the customer master and item defaults refine from there. The goal state: a rep raising an ordinary quotation never touches the tax section and it is still exactly right — because the right answer was configured, not remembered.

Change control. When FIRS moves the rate, the change is: edit the template row (with effective-date handling per accounting guidance), test on a draft, announce. One object, one edit, whole system consistent — the payoff of write-once, collected precisely when it matters most.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Item Tax Templates: exempt and zero-rated rows done right
lessons.html:
Not everything on a Nigerian invoice is standard-rated, and the professional handles mixed taxability on ONE document without breaking the arithmetic for anything else. The instrument is the Item Tax Template.

The mechanics. An Item Tax Template attaches to an ITEM (or item group) and overrides the document template's rate for that row only. The document says VAT 7.5%; the exempt item's template says VAT 0% for me; the invoice computes 7.5% on the taxable rows and 0% on that row — one document, mixed taxability, correct totals, correct liability. The rejected alternatives each break something: deleting the document's tax row zeroes EVERY row (the taxable lines now under-charge); splitting into two invoices doubles the paperwork to dodge a solved problem; faking it with a discount misstates price AND still books VAT the filing must then unwind.

Exempt vs zero-rated — the distinction that marks a professional. Both charge the customer 0% VAT; they differ on the seller's side of the ledger. Zero-rated supplies (classically exports, and specified categories) are within the VAT system at a rate of zero — the sale is a taxable supply, reported as such, with input-credit consequences the accountant cares about. Exempt supplies (Nigerian law lists basic food items, medical products and services, educational materials, among others) sit OUTSIDE the charge — no VAT charged, different reporting line, different input-credit posture. The seller's number is 0 either way; the FILING is not. Configuration follows the accountant's classification of each item class; the consultant's job is encoding that classification as item tax templates so documents get it right unattended — and knowing enough to ask the classification question rather than guessing.

Application discipline. Attach at the most stable level: an item GROUP template covers a whole exempt class (medical consumables) in one object; item-level templates handle the exceptions. Audit the mapping when the catalog grows: the new exempt item created without its template quietly charges 7.5% until a customer or an auditor notices — Chapter 9 meets that ticket, and the monthly cross-check (exempt-classified items vs items carrying the template) prevents it.

Reading a mixed invoice. The tax section shows the computed rows; per-line taxability is visible in the item tax detail. Teach clients to READ it once — the pharmacist who sees their exempt medicals at 0% and their taxable cosmetics at 7.5% on one clean invoice stops phoning about tax forever.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Inclusive vs exclusive: the arithmetic in full
lessons.html:
One checkbox separates two pricing worlds, and confusing them misstates either your price or your VAT return. This chapter makes the arithmetic reflexive in both directions.

Exclusive (the default). The entered rate is the NET price; tax adds on top. Rate ₦1,000, VAT 7.5% → tax ₦75, total ₦1,075. B2B trade lives here: procurement offices think in net prices and input credits, and your quotations (Selling 3) show net, VAT, gross as separate honest lines.

Inclusive. The tax row's inclusive setting means the entered rate already CONTAINS the tax. Rate ₦1,075 inclusive → net ₦1,000, VAT ₦75. The arithmetic, both directions, cold: net = inclusive ÷ 1.075; VAT = inclusive − net (equivalently inclusive × 7.5/107.5). Drill it: ₦2,150 inclusive → ₦2,000 net + ₦150 VAT. ₦10,750,000 inclusive → ₦10,000,000 net + ₦750,000 VAT. Retail-facing trade lives here: shelf prices are what-you-pay, and the system extracts the embedded VAT for the filing.

The two misconfiguration disasters, named. (1) Prices set as tax-inclusive but the row left EXCLUSIVE: the system adds 7.5% on top of a price that already contained it — the customer is overcharged (tax on tax), and the firm looks either greedy or incompetent at the till. (2) Prices set net but the row marked INCLUSIVE: the system carves VAT out of what was meant to be pure revenue — every sale silently yields 93.02% of its intended net, and the margin erosion hides until someone reconciles a month. Both diseases are one checkbox misaligned with one price-entry convention; the cure is a declared convention per price list (this list is inclusive; that one is net) and the checkbox matching it — checked once at setup, audited when lists are added.

One regime per document. Never mix conventions on a single document; per-list declaration keeps regimes segregated by construction, since documents inherit one list (Selling 2). Where a business genuinely runs both worlds — counter retail inclusive, B2B exclusive — that is two price lists and two document flows, each internally consistent, meeting only in the ledgers where both post exact VAT.

Presentation. Inclusive documents can still BREAK OUT the VAT in totals for the customer's paperwork (Selling 3, Chapter 4) — showing inclusive line prices and an extracted VAT figure is the honest retail-adjacent format, and it is what a VAT-registered buyer needs to claim their credit.

A worked till moment. The counter sells three items off the inclusive retail list — ₦2,150, ₦4,300, ₦1,075 shelf prices. The receipt totals ₦7,525; the totals section extracts ₦525 VAT (7,525 × 7.5/107.5) over a ₦7,000 net, and the day's VAT liability accrues to the naira without the cashier knowing the word regime. Meanwhile the B2B desk quotes the same goods off the exclusive list at their net rates plus a visible ₦525 VAT line. Same goods, same tax truth, two presentations — each native to its buyer.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Pricing Rules: anatomy & design
lessons.html:
A Pricing Rule is policy that fires itself: when conditions match, a discount or special rate applies — no memo, no memory, no rep discretion required. This chapter is the anatomy and the design doctrine.

The anatomy — three parts.

  • WHO and WHAT it applies to — conditions on the parties and goods: item, item group, or brand on one axis; customer, customer group, or territory on the other. The clean trees you built in Selling 1 and 2 are the targeting system: a rule aimed at group Distribution or territory South-West hits exactly what those trees define — mushy trees, mushy policy.
  • WHEN and HOW MUCH — quantity brackets (min/max qty: the 50-carton threshold), and validity dates (valid from/to: the Q4 window). Date-bounded rules start and STOP themselves — the promo that ends on schedule with no cleanup, the same self-executing elegance as validity-dated Item Prices (Selling 2, Chapter 6).
  • THE EFFECT — a discount percentage, a discount amount, or an outright special rate for the match.

So the running example assembles itself: 10% off, item group Beverages, customer group Distribution, min qty 50 cartons, valid 01-Oct to 31-Dec. Built once; fires on every qualifying order; dies on New Year's Day.

Priority and stacking. When several rules match one row, priority decides which applies — and rules can be set not to stack, so the winner applies alone. Design doctrine: engineer for ONE obvious winner per realistic scenario. A row where three overlapping rules fight, resolved by priority numbers nobody remembers, produces the Chapter 9 ticket — a surprising discount nobody can explain without a whiteboard. If you cannot state in one sentence which rule governs a given sale, the rule set is too clever.

Rules vs the other pricing instruments — the placement doctrine, complete. Base reality lives in price lists (Selling 2): who structurally pays what. Conditional policy lives in pricing rules: IF this buyer, this volume, this window. Genuine one-off negotiation lives in the document's Rate (Selling 3): visible, measured exceptions. Each instrument misused as another causes a known disease: rules patching stale base rates (Selling 2, Chapter 6's conviction), lists cloned per quarter to fake date-bounds, overrides doing structurally what a rule should. Place each policy at its level and every price on every document has one findable explanation.

Lifecycle. Rules are disabled when retired, never deleted while history references their period — the explanation of last Q4's pricing should remain readable next year. Few, legible, dated, owned: the four adjectives of a healthy rule set.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Discounts governance
lessons.html:
Discounts are where pricing policy meets human nature; governance is what keeps the meeting civilised. This chapter assembles the controls you have met into one posture.

The three instruments, at policy altitude. Selling 3 distinguished them mechanically; here is who should hold each. The row discount percentage / Rate edit — the negotiator's tool, for genuine per-deal concession, always visible against Price List Rate. The Additional Discount — a document-level cut on net or grand total: the whole-deal gesture (the MD shaving ₦200k off a ₦9.7m package to close), rare by nature, glaring by design — which is its virtue: nobody additional-discounts quietly. And pricing rules — policy discounts that fire themselves (Chapter 5), which is where anything RECURRING belongs.

The escalation ladder. A healthy shop runs concessions up a ladder: list price → rule-given discount (automatic, no approval needed — it IS the approval, pre-granted) → the rep's negotiated margin within a known band → beyond the band, escalation to the sales lead — and the floor under the whole ladder is Validate Selling Price Against Purchase Rate (Selling 8), the below-cost block that makes the worst outcome impossible at the keyboard. Where approval workflows are configured, the band is enforced by the system; where they are not, the band is enforced by the review — either way there IS a band, stated, known.

Measurement — the governance that actually governs. Because every concession is visible (Rate vs Price List Rate; additional discounts as fields; rules as named objects), discount behaviour is REPORTABLE: realised discount by rep, by customer, by item group, by period. The monthly read answers the questions that matter: who concedes most, to whom, and did the volume justify it? The pathological reading it catches early: the discount-everything culture — when average realised discount creeps up quarter on quarter, list prices have quietly stopped being prices, and the fix is Selling 2's repricing plus a re-anchored band, not another memo.

Free goods, restated as governance. The two-row treatment (100 at rate + 20 at zero, Selling 3) is a governance feature: free quantity is VISIBLE quantity — countable in stock (the 20 really left), attributable in reports (who gives away how much), and honest at the gate. Bundled free goods hidden in doctored rates fail all three at once.

The posture in one sentence. Structure in lists, policy in rules, exceptions on documents, a floor in configuration, and a monthly mirror in reporting — a firm holding that posture can negotiate hard all day without ever losing track of what its prices are.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The invoice bridge
lessons.html:
The Sales Invoice deserves — and has — its own full module: Selling 7 treats creation paths, statuses, Payment Entries, advances, write-offs and credit notes at manual depth. This chapter is the bridge: what THIS module's tax-and-pricing machinery hands to it, and the working vocabulary you need before crossing.

The accounting event, located. On the timeline law (Selling 5): order reserves, delivery deducts, invoice books, payment settles. Submitting the Sales Invoice books revenue and the customer's receivable — and, this module's addition: it also crystallises the VAT. The template you configured (Chapters 1-2), the item overrides (Chapter 3), the inclusive/exclusive regime (Chapter 4), the rule-given and negotiated discounts (Chapters 5-6) — all of them converge on the invoice, whose tax rows post to the liability account that the monthly filing reads. Everything upstream was policy; the invoice is where policy becomes a ledger fact FIRS can ask about.

Creation, one sentence each. From the order (billing ahead or alongside — the Montaigne advance) or from the DN (billing exactly what shipped) — the create-from spine unbroken; Selling 7 Chapter 1 gives the full treatment including the standalone and Update-Stock cases and their traps.

Status vocabulary, for reading lists today. Unpaid → Partly Paid → Paid; Overdue the moment the due date passes unpaid; Credit Note Issued when a return invoice stands against it. Enough to read any invoice list correctly; the collections craft built on it is Selling 7 Chapters 2-4.

Two handoffs to carry across the bridge. First, the To-Bill worklist: Selling 5 left delivered-unbilled DNs as a quiet alarm; the invoice is the answer, and Selling 7 formalises the oldest-first routine with an owner and a measured DN-to-invoice-days metric. Second, the credit note: Selling 5, Chapter 7 reversed stock on the return DN and named its money half — the Sales Invoice with Is Return, against the original — whose full mechanics (statuses, correction doctrine, the FIRS-grade audit pairing) are Selling 7 Chapter 4. Hold the pairing sentence until then: stock reverses on the return DN; money reverses on the credit note.

Why the split matters. Tax-and-pricing is POLICY work — configured by consultants, owned by accountants, invisible to good reps. Invoicing-and-collections is OPERATING work — daily, human, cash-critical. One module per altitude; the bridge is the invoice they share.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The three watching reports
lessons.html:
Configuration without reading is faith; this chapter is the reading. Three reports, one weekly habit, and the commercial review they feed. A sales professional who reads these weekly manages a book; one who does not, gets managed by it.

Sales Analytics — what is selling, to whom, where. Revenue cut by customer, item, item group, customer group, or territory, across time periods — every dimension you disciplined in Selling 1-2 now pays rent. The three reads to practice: trend (this quarter vs last, per cut — growth and its location); mix (which groups carry the number — the Services share your recurring-revenue story lives in); and the read that saves relationships: the quietly shrinking customer — an account down 30% across three periods announces churn a year before it resigns, and the response is a next step on the pipeline (your own cadence machinery), not a shrug at year-end. Group by customer, sort by decline, act on the top five: fifteen minutes that outperform most CRM dashboards.

Sales Order Analysis — the promise backlog. Ordered vs delivered vs billed across all open orders: the company's delivery backlog on one screen, readable by amount and by age. This report — not the DN list (Selling 5 taught why: DNs record what DID ship) — answers what stands promised and unperformed. The reads: overdue-to-promise rows (the delivery-date discipline of Selling 4 making lateness visible); the delivered-not-billed column (the To-Bill leak, quantified in naira); and per-customer slices for the account conversations. Warehouse planning, billing chase, and customer honesty all drink from this one well.

Accounts Receivable — who owes what, aged. Outstanding per customer, bucketed 0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 90+ days. The professional read is right to left: the 90+ column first (each entry a story with a name — dispute? distress? neglect?), then 61-90 (this month's interventions, before they graduate rightward), then the near buckets (the healthy hum). Left-to-right reading — admiring the big healthy 0-30 — is the complacency read; the money that kills firms is always in the right-hand columns, aging politely. Every right-column entry gets an owner and a dated next step (Selling 7 builds the full collections craft on exactly this).

The cadence and the page. Weekly, thirty minutes, all three — and quarterly, ONE page for the commercial review: revenue trend and mix (Analytics), backlog and slippage (Order Analysis), ageing shape (AR), beside the pipeline and lost-reason reads from Selling 3. One page, five graphs, every number traceable to documents. Boards steer on it; the alternative is anecdote with a projector.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Case study & support patterns
lessons.html:
First the build, then the scar tissue — HealthTrade (Selling 2's dual-channel vendor) gets its full tax-and-pricing layer, and then the seven tickets this layer generates in the wild.

THE BUILD. Step 1 — the VAT spine (Ch. 1-2): one standard template — VAT, On Net Total, 7.5%, posting to the VAT output liability the accountant confirmed — set as default; a delivery-charge variant for the routes that bill freight, its Actual row posting to freight recovery, never the VAT head. Step 2 — the exempt class (Ch. 3): medical consumables are exempt per the accountant's classification — one Item Tax Template at the item-group level covers the whole class at 0%; cosmetics and equipment stay standard. A test invoice mixing both shows 7.5% and 0% rows computing side by side, and the pharmacist-facing print is clean. Step 3 — the regimes (Ch. 4): the counter retail list is declared INCLUSIVE (shelf prices are what-you-pay; the checkbox matches), B2B lists stay exclusive; the ₦2,150 shelf item books ₦2,000 net + ₦150 VAT without a human thinking. Step 4 — the Q4 rule (Ch. 5): 10% off, Beverages group, Distribution group, min 50 cartons, 01-Oct to 31-Dec — one object; it will die on schedule. Step 5 — the governance frame (Ch. 6): below-cost validation on; the negotiation band stated (reps to 5%, lead to 12%); the monthly discount read scheduled. Step 6 — first reads (Ch. 8): month one's Analytics shows the mix baseline; Order Analysis quantifies a ₦4.1m delivered-not-billed leak (fixed by Thursday); AR's right columns are, for now, empty — the goal is keeping them so.

THE PATTERNS. 1 — VAT found typed inside item rates: the pre-system habit imported (Ch. 1); prices misstated, liability unfiled as a number; fix by re-basing prices net (or declaring inclusive properly) and letting the template compute. 2 — a tax row deleted to exempt one item: every row on the document went to zero (Ch. 3); the taxable lines under-charged; fix with the Item Tax Template and re-issue. 3 — margins mysteriously 7% thin on one list: the inclusive checkbox on a net-priced list (Ch. 4, disaster two); realign convention and checkbox, reprice the damage window. 4 — a surprising discount nobody can explain: rule stacking with forgotten priorities (Ch. 5); fix by simplifying to one-obvious-winner and disabling the fossils. 5 — average realised discount creeping quarterly: the discount-everything culture (Ch. 6); the fix is repricing plus a re-anchored band — a commercial decision the report forced into daylight. 6 — the filing figure disagrees with the invoice register: something posted to the VAT head that was not document VAT, or a template mis-aimed (Ch. 1-2); reconcile the account to the register monthly so the 21st is never a surprise. 7 — the AR read as good news while 90+ grows: left-to-right complacency (Ch. 8); institute the right-to-left read with owners on every right-column name.

The fifth law. Selling 1-2: documents are downstream of masters. Selling 3: the pipeline is downstream of discipline. Selling 4: the order is the single source of fulfilment truth. Selling 5: the DN is where the word meets the world. This module: tax and price are POLICY — encode once, apply everywhere, and audit by report. A firm that holds this law negotiates freely, files calmly, and explains any number on any document in one sentence; a firm that does not, improvises both its prices and its taxes — and eventually explains itself to FIRS instead.

sales_invoice.title: Selling 7 — The Sales Invoice, Payments & Collections
sales_invoice.desc: The accounting event in full: creating invoices from orders and delivery notes, what submission books, due dates and payment terms, Payment Entry mechanics including advances and allocation, credit notes, and the receivables discipline that turns sales into cash.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The invoice as the accounting event
lessons.html:
Everything in Selling 1-6 was preparation for this document. The Sales Invoice is where money becomes real on the books: submitting it books revenue and the customer's receivable into the general ledger, dated by its posting date, and — Selling 6's addition — crystallises the VAT to the liability account the monthly filing reads. Nothing else does this: the order promised, the DN moved goods, the payment (later) settles what the invoice creates. When any question begins when do the books recognise…, the answer is: at invoice submission.

The ledger effect, spelled out. One submission posts: debit the customer's receivable (they owe you the gross), credit revenue (the net), credit VAT output (the tax) — and, in perpetual-stock configurations, the cost-of-goods entries ride the stock movement's valuation. A Sales Professional does not journal these; the point is to KNOW they happen, so that every conversation with the accountant, the auditor, or FIRS starts from the same picture.

Creation paths, chosen by flow:

  • From the Sales Order — billing ahead of or alongside delivery: the advance and milestone flows (the Montaigne 50/40/10, Chapter 9). The order's billed-quantity ledger counts down; the To-Deliver status keeps the physical promise visible after finance is satisfied (Selling 4).
  • From the Delivery Note — billing exactly what shipped: partial-delivery trade's honest path. The invoice quantities ARE the shipped quantities; the DN advances from To Bill toward Completed.
  • Standalone — for genuinely document-less sales; rare and suspicious in disciplined B2B, because a standalone invoice counts against no order and closes no DN.

The Update Stock invoice — full treatment of the trap. An invoice with Update Stock ticked moves inventory itself, playing delivery note and invoice in one document. Its legitimate homes: counter sales and cash-and-carry, service jobs consuming materials, any flow that deliberately skips the DN. The trap, precisely: tick it on an invoice made FROM a Delivery Note and stock deducts TWICE — once at the DN, once at the invoice — and the stock report begins lying by exactly the doubled quantities. The rule: in the standard flow (order → DN → invoice), Update Stock stays OFF; where it is ON, there is no DN in that flow at all. Auditing a client's flows for this one checkbox has recovered entire phantom-stock mysteries.

Two dates, permanently distinct. The posting date is when the books record the sale; the due date is when the customer must pay. They are computed differently, serve different masters, and conflating them is the root of half of all ageing-report confusion. The due date's engineering is Chapter 2's entire subject.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Payment terms & due-date engineering
lessons.html:
The due date is not typed; it is ENGINEERED — from Payment Terms that were agreed before the invoice existed. This chapter is that engineering, because the collections craft of Chapter 8 is only as strong as the dates it enforces.

The Payment Terms Template. A named schedule of when portions of an invoice fall due: Net 30 (100% at 30 days from posting); 50% Advance, Balance Net 15; the Montaigne 50/40/10 (50% in advance, 40% on delivery, 10% on commissioning — a three-portion template). Each portion carries its share and its due rule (days after posting, day-of-following-month, etc.). Build the firm's real commercial offers as templates ONCE; the sales floor then selects agreements, never invents arithmetic.

The inheritance chain. Terms flow: customer master → sales order → invoice. Set Net-45 on MediPlus's master (Selling 1, Chapter 8) and every order inherits it, every invoice computes its due date from it, and nobody decides terms at billing time — which is the governance point: terms are AGREED at relationship or deal level, with whatever approval that took, and billing merely executes the agreement. An invoice whose terms were improvised at creation is an agreement nobody made.

Due-date computation. From posting date plus the template's rule, per portion. A ₦10m invoice on 50% Advance / Balance Net 30, posted 1 September: ₦5m due immediately, ₦5m due 1 October — TWO schedule rows on one invoice, and the ageing report (Chapter 8) ages each portion by its own due date. This is why multi-portion templates beat splitting into multiple invoices: one invoice, one document for the customer's records, a schedule the system enforces portion by portion.

Retention — the 10% that waits. Project and installation trade holds a retention: the final portion due on commissioning, sign-off, or a defects period. Model it as the template's last portion with its longer rule — the Montaigne 10% is exactly this — so the retained amount ages correctly as NOT-YET-DUE rather than polluting the overdue columns, and surfaces on schedule when its trigger date arrives. Retentions tracked in someone's memory are retentions never collected; the schedule row is the memory.

Credit days and the limit. Terms interact with the credit limit (Selling 1, Chapter 6): longer terms mean more exposure per naira of monthly sales — the ₦15m limit that fits Net-30 strangles the same customer on Net-60. When terms are renegotiated, the limit review rides along; the two numbers are one risk decision wearing two fields.

Discipline summary. Templates for every real offer; terms on masters and orders, never improvised on invoices; multi-portion schedules for staged deals; retention as the last portion. Do this, and Chapter 8's collections machine runs on dates a court would recognise.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Statuses & reading the invoice book
lessons.html:
The invoice list, read correctly, is the firm's cash cockpit. This chapter is the vocabulary and the worklists.

The status vocabulary, complete:

  • Draft — being prepared; no ledger effect yet.
  • Unpaid — submitted; the receivable stands; no money allocated.
  • Partly Paid — some allocation received; outstanding visible. A ₦2m receipt against ₦5m leaves exactly this — never Paid, and no longer merely Unpaid.
  • Paid — outstanding cleared to zero (allocations plus any write-off, Chapter 6).
  • Overdue — the due date (or a portion's due date) passed while an outstanding remains. Automatic, merciless, and the single most useful filter in the module.
  • Credit Note Issued — a return invoice stands against it (Chapter 7).
  • Return — the credit note itself carries this, marking it as the reversal side.
  • Cancelled — the document lifecycle exit; its ledger entries reversed by cancellation, its number retained in history.

The three worklists, from one list:

  • Overdue, oldest first — collections (Chapter 8 operationalises it). Every entry is money the firm has EARNED and not received; the sort order is the priority order.
  • Unpaid, due this week — the pre-emptive list: a polite reminder BEFORE the due date converts more invoices than a firm letter after it. Nigerian B2B pays the supplier who asks on time.
  • Draft older than a day — the leak inside the house: invoices prepared and never submitted book nothing, age nowhere, and hide from every report. Drafts are a workspace, not a warehouse.

The To-Bill handoff, formalised. Selling 5 left delivered-unbilled DNs as an alarm; here is the standing routine. The owner: a named person (in an 11-person firm, the accountant or ops lead — named, not implied). The cadence: daily or twice-weekly, the To-Bill DN list oldest first, each becoming an invoice FROM its DN or carrying a written reason it cannot yet. The metric: DN-to-invoice days — median days between delivery and invoice submission. World-class is same-day to two days; a creeping median is the earliest possible warning that revenue is leaking between the warehouse and finance, visible weeks before it shows as a cash problem. Measure it, post it, and the handoff gap that Chapter 10 meets as a disease never forms.

The account view. Per-customer, all invoices, all statuses, schedule rows visible: the screen for the terms conversation, the statement dispute, the credit-limit review. Selling 4 gave account owners the promises screen; this is its cash twin — together they are the whole relationship on two tabs.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Payment Entry I: receiving money
lessons.html:
Money arrives; the Payment Entry records it — and records it in a way the BANK STATEMENT will recognise, which is the standard this chapter holds throughout.

Creation. From the invoice: Create > Payment — party, references and amounts pre-fill, and the entry is born allocated. The fields that matter:

  • Mode of Payment — transfer, POS, cash, cheque. Not decoration: modes map to accounts and to reconciliation behaviour, and a firm that records mode honestly can answer how much cash did the counter take Tuesday without a drawer count.
  • Paid To (the bank account) — the actual account the money entered. THE reconciliation field: month-end bank rec is matching entries to statement lines, and entries pointing at the wrong bank are the archaeology.
  • Reference number and date — the transfer reference, the teller number, the cheque number. Sixty seconds at entry; hours saved per dispute.
  • Allocation rows — which invoices, how much each. The entry's heart, and Chapter 5's subject at depth.

Full payment. Allocation equals outstanding; the invoice flips to Paid. The base case, worth one sentence.

Partial payment. Allocate what came; the invoice stands Partly Paid, outstanding visible and aging by its due date. Repeat as receipts arrive — three payments against one invoice are three entries, each matching a real bank line. Resist the anti-pattern of holding receipts unrecorded until the customer finishes paying: cash in the bank unrecorded in the ledger is the reconciliation break you built yourself.

The bank-line law. One real-world receipt = one Payment Entry. A customer's single ₦12m transfer is ONE entry (however many invoices it settles — Chapter 5); three separate cheques are THREE entries even if they arrived in one envelope. Entries mirror bank lines; when they do, reconciliation is a matching game; when they do not — receipts merged for convenience, or one transfer split into fabricated entries — every month-end begins with an investigation.

Journals are not receipts. A bare journal entry crediting the customer records a number while orphaning everything the Payment Entry carries: no reference, no mode, no allocation to specific invoices, no place in payment reports. Journals have their accounting uses; recording customer receipts is not one of them, and Chapter 10 meets the ledger that thought otherwise.

Posting date honesty, again. The entry's date is when the money moved — the statement's date, not the recording afternoon's. The same chronology law as the DN (Selling 5): ledgers are believed exactly as far as their dates are true.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Payment Entry II: advances, allocation & multi-invoice
lessons.html:
Real receipts rarely match one invoice neatly. This chapter is the allocation craft — the difference between a receivables ledger that answers questions and one that generates them.

One payment, many invoices. The ₦12m transfer settling four invoices: ONE Payment Entry, four allocation rows splitting the amount across the references — each invoice's outstanding reduced by its share, each flipping to Paid or Partly Paid as its share dictates. Which invoices, in what order? The default craft: oldest first, unless the customer's remittance advice says otherwise — and when it says otherwise, FOLLOW the advice and keep it on file, because allocation against the customer's instruction is how two correct ledgers come to disagree, and Chapter 10's allocation-drift disease is born from exactly this shortcut.

The advance — money before any invoice. Your enterprise reality: 50% before work begins. The mechanics: a Payment Entry against the customer with no invoice reference — the amount sits as an advance (unallocated credit) on the customer's account, visible in their balance, reducing their net exposure, waiting. It is NOT parked in a drawer until an invoice exists (unrecorded cash), NOT a negative invoice, NOT a discount promised against future billing.

Allocation — the advance meets its invoice. When the invoice is raised, the advance is allocated to it — pulled into the invoice's settlement so the outstanding nets down. The Montaigne flow in miniature: ₦4.85m advance received (entry against customer); first invoice ₦4.85m raised from the order; allocation applied; invoice Paid; advance consumed. The failure mode this discipline prevents is expensive and common: the advance sits unallocated forever, the invoice is paid by a fresh receipt or chased as overdue, and the customer is functionally double-credited — or rightly furious at being dunned for money they sent months ago. Chapter 10 names it the unallocated-advance black hole; the prevention is a standing monthly read of unallocated credits per customer, each one matched to its invoice or explained.

Partial allocation and mixed entries. An advance may cover part of a larger invoice (allocate the advance, balance stays outstanding on schedule); one entry may combine allocation to old invoices AND an advance residue for future ones — the rows express it exactly. The ledger's job is to mirror the commercial reality however untidy; the craft is expressing untidiness precisely rather than rounding it into fiction.

Refunding an advance. The deal dies after the deposit: the advance is refunded by a payment OUT against the customer, consuming the credit — documented, referenced, mirrored in the bank. Never a quiet journal, never keep it against something future unless the customer has agreed in writing to exactly that.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Write-offs, deductions & Nigerian short-pay realities
lessons.html:
The amount that arrives is often not the amount invoiced — and in Nigerian B2B, the difference is frequently LAWFUL. This chapter is the taxonomy of short payments and the exact treatment of each; mishandling them is the fastest way to fill an ageing report with fictional debts.

Reality one: Withholding Tax (WHT) deducted at source. The big one. Qualifying Nigerian customers — companies, government — are REQUIRED to withhold tax from certain payments (services and contracts prominently; rates commonly 5% for corporate service arrangements, with other categories at other rates — the firm's accountant owns the exact schedule) and remit it to FIRS on your behalf. So Montaigne, invoiced ₦1,000,000 for services, lawfully pays ₦950,000 and remits ₦50,000 to FIRS against your tax identity, issuing (eventually) a WHT credit note/certificate — which is REAL MONEY to you: creditable against your company income tax.

The treatment, exactly: the Payment Entry records ₦950,000 received, allocates the FULL ₦1,000,000 to the invoice, and carries the ₦50,000 as a deduction row posting to a WHT receivable asset account. The invoice closes Paid (the customer's obligation to YOU is fully discharged — part in cash, part in tax paid on your behalf); the receivable ledger is clean; and the WHT receivable account accumulates the certificates-to-chase balance. The wrong treatments, each with its cost: leaving ₦50,000 outstanding forever (a fictional debt that poisons the ageing and eventually gets dunned — embarrassing both firms); writing it off (donating a tax credit); a credit note (there was no return and no error — the price was right). The certificate chase is then a standing discipline: the WHT receivable is only worth its paper, so certificates are requested, logged against their deductions, and handed to the accountant for the income-tax credit — a monthly list, owned, like everything else in this module.

Reality two: bank charges on the receipt. The transfer arrives ₦4,850 light because a bank took its fee in transit. Same instrument: full allocation to the invoice, a deduction row posting the charge to bank-charges expense. The invoice closes; the expense lands where expenses live.

Reality three: the genuine short-pay. ₦1,999,820 against ₦2m — rounding, a customer's payment-run quirk, no dispute intended. Within the firm's configured write-off limit, the Payment Entry writes off the ₦180 to the write-off account and closes the invoice honestly. Chasing ₦180 forever costs more than ₦180; carrying it as outstanding pollutes every report it touches. Above the limit, it is not a write-off — it is either a dispute (Chapter 8's process) or an agreed adjustment (Chapter 7's credit note); the limit exists precisely to keep those categories from blurring.

What is NEVER the treatment: editing the invoice total to match the receipt. The invoice is the record of what was agreed and billed; the Payment Entry's deduction machinery exists so that every difference between billed and banked is CLASSIFIED — tax, charge, write-off — and lands in its own account with its own trail. An invoice edited to meet its payment has destroyed the only evidence of the difference.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Credit notes & the correction doctrine
lessons.html:
Submitted invoices are never edited and never deleted — their immutability is what makes the ledger evidence. Reversal and correction happen through the credit note, and this chapter is its complete mechanics plus the doctrine around it.

The instrument. A credit note is a Sales Invoice with Is Return ticked, made against the original invoice, carrying negative amounts: revenue reversed, VAT reversed, the receivable reduced — each by exactly the credited quantities and values, each linked to what it reverses. The original's status flips to Credit Note Issued; the credit note itself carries Return. Two documents, permanently married in the record.

The two occasions:

  • Returned goods — the money half of Selling 5's pairing: stock came back on the return DN; the credit note gives the money back its mirror. Raise it against the original invoice for the returned quantities — partial returns get partial credit notes, the linkage keeping every remainder honest. The pairing sentence, final form: stock reverses on the return DN; money reverses on the credit note; one physical event, two ledgers, two linked documents.
  • Billing corrections — wrong rate, wrong quantity, wrong customer even. The doctrine: credit note against the wrong invoice, then re-invoice correctly. Both documents stand forever: every figure that ever hit the ledger PLUS the visible instrument that unwound it. This is precisely what auditors and FIRS expect to find; the alternative culture — journals quietly patching invoice errors, or administrative edits to submitted documents — is what turns a routine audit forensic, because a ledger that can be silently corrected is a ledger that proves nothing.

What the customer does with a credit. Two lawful endings: the credit is applied against other invoices (allocated like a payment — the customer's next settlement nets it off), or refunded (a payment out, referenced, banked — Chapter 5's refund mechanics). Which one is the customer's call within the commercial relationship; the system's job is that the credit exists as a first-class balance until one ending consumes it — never an off-ledger IOU, never we will remember at the next order.

Credit notes and the VAT return. The reversed VAT flows back through the liability account — the month's filing nets it automatically because the credit note is a document like any other (Selling 6's architecture paying off in reverse). A credit given outside the system, by discount-on-the-next-invoice handshake, misstates two months' VAT at once.

Governance. Credit notes are powerful — they erase receivables — so they carry the same visibility posture as discounts (Selling 6): a monthly read of credit notes by value, reason, and raiser. A firm whose credit-note report is boring is a firm whose billing is accurate; a spike is either a quality problem upstream (returns — route to operations) or a billing-discipline problem inside (corrections — route to training). Either way the report knew first.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The collections craft
lessons.html:
Selling ends when the money is in the bank; collections is the craft of the last mile. It is a SYSTEM — cadence, instruments, escalation — not a mood that strikes when cash feels tight. This chapter builds the system.

The posture. Collections begins before anything is late: terms agreed on the offer (Selling 3), enforced dates engineered (Chapter 2), invoices submitted same-day-as-delivery (Chapter 3's metric). A firm that bills promptly and reminds politely is PAID first in its customers' payment runs — Nigerian B2B triages suppliers by who is organised, and everything below is that organisation made visible.

The weekly engine, four gears:

  • Gear 1 — the pre-due reminder. Invoices due within 7 days get a courteous note with the invoice attached. Cost: minutes. Effect: your invoice is IN the payment run instead of after it.
  • Gear 2 — the statement. Monthly, every credit customer receives a Statement of Account: invoices, credits, payments, balance. Customers dispute what they see quarterly; they PAY what they see monthly — and the statement surfaces allocation disagreements (Chapter 5) while they are one month deep, not eight.
  • Gear 3 — the overdue ladder. AR read right-to-left (Selling 6, Chapter 8), each right-column entry worked up a stated ladder: reminder → call with a promise-to-pay recorded — and in this house a promise-to-pay IS a dated next step on the board, with an owner, that fires (your v3.75 reminder machinery doing collections duty) → escalation letter → commercial measures.
  • Gear 4 — the commercial measures. The credit machinery from Selling 1 and 4, now used: the credit limit blocks new exposure automatically as outstandings swell; open orders go on Hold (Selling 4, Chapter 5) pending payment — the polite sentence is we have paused the next delivery while the account catches up, and it collects better than any letter because it is not a threat, it is a system behaving predictably.

Disputes, quarantined. A genuinely disputed invoice (wrong goods claim, pricing disagreement) is FLAGGED and worked as a dispute — investigation, resolution by credit note or by evidence — and NOT dunned while flagged: dunning a dispute hardens it. But the flag has an owner and an age limit; disputes are a queue, not a parking lot, and the monthly read includes disputes older than 30 days by name.

The metrics that steer. Three numbers, monthly: DSO (days sales outstanding — the book's overall speed); ageing shape (the % beyond 60 days — the risk concentration); promise-kept rate (of recorded promises-to-pay, how many landed — which tells you whose word prices at par). Post them where the commercial team sees them; collections improves fastest when it is measured in public and worked in private.

The tone. Every instrument above is polite, predictable, and relentless — the three adjectives that collect. Anger is amateur; silence is expensive; the system is neither.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Case study: the Montaigne billing, settled to zero
lessons.html:
The deal that began as a quotation in Selling 3, committed in Selling 4, and shipped its waves in Selling 5 now runs its money to zero — through an advance, staged invoices, a lawful WHT deduction, a credit note, and a retention. Every chapter clocks in.

The frame (Ch. 2). Order value ₦9.7m on the 50/40/10 template: ₦4.85m advance, ₦3.88m on delivery, ₦970k retention on commissioning. The schedule lives on the terms; the invoices will inherit it.

Step 1 — the advance (Ch. 5). Before wave one ships, Montaigne transfers ₦4.85m. Payment Entry against the customer, no invoice yet — reference captured, bank account exact — sitting as an unallocated advance. The advance invoice is then raised FROM the order for the 50% portion; the advance is allocated; invoice Paid; credit consumed. (The Selling 4 hold episode — the four-day stall in Montaigne's approval chain — happened exactly here, and released here.)

Step 2 — wave billing (Ch. 1, 3). As each delivery wave completes, its invoice is raised from the DNs — billing exactly what shipped, branch by branch; the To-Bill DNs clear within a day (the metric holds at same-day), and the order's billed ledger climbs alongside its delivered ledger. Update Stock stays OFF throughout — the DNs moved the stock; the invoices move only money.

Step 3 — the lawful short-pay (Ch. 6). The 40% invoice (₦3.88m, service-heavy) is settled by Montaigne at ₦3.686m — 5% WHT of ₦194k withheld at source. The Payment Entry: ₦3.686m received, FULL ₦3.88m allocated, ₦194k deduction to the WHT receivable. Invoice Paid; ageing clean; and the certificate chase begins — logged, owned, requested with the same politeness as everything else, because that paper is creditable tax.

Step 4 — the DOA credit (Ch. 7). Selling 5's damaged terminal (T-88214, quarantined; T-88519 shipped as replacement) resolves commercially as a like-for-like swap: the replacement was invoiced on its wave, so a credit note against that wave's invoice for one terminal reverses the double-billing — negative quantities, linked to the original, the wave invoice flipping to Credit Note Issued for that line's value. Montaigne elects to apply the credit against the retention invoice rather than take a refund — noted, and waiting.

Step 5 — the retention (Ch. 2, 8). Commissioning signs off in week 10; the retention portion falls due ON SCHEDULE — it aged as not-yet-due the whole time, polluting nothing. The ₦970k invoice is raised; the parked credit allocates against it; the balance arrives inside terms after one pre-due reminder (Gear 1 earning its keep).

Step 6 — zero (Ch. 3, 5). The account view reads: every invoice Paid, no unallocated credits, WHT receivable carrying its ₦194k awaiting certificate, order Completed-and-Closed at 11 sets (Selling 4's honest ending). One deal, five modules, and any colleague can reconstruct every naira of it from the documents alone — which is the entire point of the machine.

The ledger of the deal: ₦9.7m committed → ₦8.897m banked + ₦194k in tax paid on the firm's behalf + ₦609k credited for the swap-and-retention netting — and not one number lives in anyone's memory.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Support patterns & the sixth law
lessons.html:
The cash module's scar tissue — the most expensive tickets in the entire manual, because every disease here IS money. Symptom → disease → fix.

Pattern 1 — stock report wrong by exactly the recent sales. Update Stock ticked on DN-based invoices (Ch. 1): every sale deducted twice. Fix: untick and correct the movements; audit the flow for which document owns deduction. The one-checkbox phantom-stock generator.

Pattern 2 — receipts recorded as journal entries. The pre-system habit (Ch. 4): balances roughly right, but no references, no modes, no allocations — reconciliation impossible, payment reports empty, and specific invoices still showing outstanding while the account nets fine. Fix: re-book as Payment Entries against their invoices; retire the habit with training, not memos.

Pattern 3 — the unallocated-advance black hole. Advances taken, never allocated (Ch. 5): customers dunned for invoices their deposits already covered, or double-credited when fresh receipts settle what the advance should have. Fix: the monthly unallocated-credits read, each matched to its invoice or explained; apologise to whoever got dunned — they were right.

Pattern 4 — the ageing full of fictional WHT debts. Lawful withholdings left as outstanding balances (Ch. 6): the 5% tails of every service invoice aging into the 90+ column, poisoning DSO, and eventually dunned — embarrassing the firm to its best corporate customers. Fix: re-book each with the deduction treatment to the WHT receivable; institute the certificate chase; teach the taxonomy of short-pays so cash application classifies instead of parks.

Pattern 5 — a submitted invoice was edited to match its payment. The evidence-destruction culture (Ch. 6, 7): the difference between billed and banked is now unexplainable forever. Fix: revert; classify the difference properly (deduction, write-off, or credit note); close the administrative permission that allowed it — and as with Selling 4's Pattern 7, this escalates as governance, because a quietly editable ledger proves nothing.

Pattern 6 — credit note raised with no return DN (or the reverse). The pairing broken (Ch. 7; Selling 5): money reversed while stock did not come back, or goods returned while the customer still owes the price. Each half-event leaves one ledger lying. Fix: complete the pair — the missing document, linked to its original — and reconcile the gap period.

Pattern 7 — allocation drift. Payments allocated by convenience against the customer's remittance advice (Ch. 5): both ledgers correct in total, disagreeing per invoice; every statement triggers a dispute about WHICH invoices are open. Fix: reallocate to match the advices on file; adopt the follow-the-advice rule; send statements monthly so drift surfaces at one month deep.

The sixth law. Selling 1-2: documents are downstream of masters. Selling 3: the pipeline is downstream of discipline. Selling 4: the order is the single source of fulfilment truth. Selling 5: the DN is where the word meets the world. Selling 6: tax and price are policy. This module: the invoice ledger is the cash truth, and collections is a system, not a mood. Every naira billed is classified on arrival — cash, tax withheld, charge, write-off, credit — every date is real, every promise has an owner, and the firm that holds this law is paid first, files calmly, and never argues with its own books.

Due date is the delivery date

A journal to patch the ledger

advanced.title: Selling 8 — Advanced Selling: Settings, Bundles, Blanket Orders & Sales Teams
advanced.desc: The advanced layer: Selling Settings in depth, Product Bundles, Blanket Orders for long-term rate agreements, and the two sales-team structures — Sales Person (internal, contribution and targets) and Sales Partner (external channel and commission).

lessons.title: Selling Settings — the full tour
lessons.html:
Selling Settings is where selling policy becomes system behaviour. A consultant should be able to defend every switch on this screen to a client's managing director. The tour:

Naming: Customer Naming By — Customer Name makes the record's ID the name itself ("Alpha Pharmacy"); Naming Series issues CUST-00042 style IDs. The decision rule: chains and portfolios with duplicate or near-duplicate names need the series — a retailer with "Adepoju Stores" in three cities cannot key records by name without collisions. Series naming keeps identity unambiguous forever; the display name remains human.

Defaults: Default Customer Group, Territory, and Selling Price List pre-fill new records and documents. Set them to your commonest case so hurried data entry lands correctly instead of blank.

The discipline switches — each answers a client policy question:

  • "Can we stop staff typing special prices?" → untick Allow User to Edit Price List Rate. Rates then come ONLY from Item Price records; the rate field is read-only on documents. The single strongest anti-discount control that exists — stronger than memos, smaller price lists, or threats.
  • "Can we prevent selling below cost?" → Validate Selling Price Against Purchase Rate: blocks a selling rate below the item's purchase cost at the point of entry. Margin protection built into the keyboard, not discovered in a month-end report.
  • "Can the agreed rate change between order and invoice?" → Maintain Same Rate Throughout Sales Cycle, whose companion action setting chooses the response to a drift: Stop (hard block) or Warning (allow but flag). Strict shops choose Stop; shops with legitimate mid-cycle repricing choose Warning. Not silence, not auto-correction, not an email.
  • Allow Item to be Added Multiple Times — same item on two rows (standard + promo rate), from Selling 1.
  • The global over-delivery allowance — the fallback that Selling 4's per-item tolerance overrides.

When a policy question arrives, check this screen before writing a customisation — nine times in ten, the switch already exists.

lessons.title: Product Bundles
lessons.html:
You price as ONE thing but pick as MANY things: a "Pharmacy Starter Pack" at ₦450,000 that is really shelving units + a barcode scanner + a receipt printer. The Product Bundle is the correct model — never a workaround stock item whose contents live in someone's head and whose warehouse quantity nobody can honestly count.

The construction:

  • The parent item — created as a normal item BUT non-stock: Maintain Stock UNTICKED. The parent never has warehouse quantity; it is a commercial identity, not a physical one. (Not "a stock item with quantity", not necessarily serialized, not a service.)
  • The bundle definition — the Product Bundle record lists the parent and its child items with quantities: 4 × shelf unit, 1 × scanner, 1 × printer.
  • Pricing — an Item Price for the PARENT on your selling list: ₦450,000. Children need no selling price for the bundle to work.

The mechanics at each document: on the quotation and the invoice, the customer sees ONE line at the parent's price — clean commercial presentation, no per-child price exposure. On the Delivery Note, the bundle EXPLODES into its packed items — the children appear as the packed-items list, and it is the CHILDREN that move stock from the warehouse: 4 shelves, 1 scanner, 1 printer deducted; the parent deducts nothing (it has nothing to deduct). Price lives on the parent; picking lives on the children. Hampers, promo packs, starter kits, installation kits — the pattern is everywhere in Nigerian retail; model it once, correctly.

lessons.title: Blanket Orders
lessons.html:
A customer says: "we'll take 10,000 cartons over the next six months — what's your best rate?" You agree ₦820. This is more than a quotation (they've committed, not enquired) and less than a Sales Order (they don't want 10,000 cartons delivered Tuesday). It is a Blanket Order: a long-term rate-and-quantity agreement consumed over time.

Creating it: the Blanket Order carries the customer, the items with agreed quantities and agreed rates, and the from/to dates of the agreement. Submitting it creates no reservation and moves no stock — it establishes the commercial frame.

Drawing against it: each real purchase becomes an ordinary Sales Order referencing the blanket order — and two things happen automatically: the order row inherits the agreed ₦820 rate (nobody negotiates twice, nobody "forgets" the deal rate), and the blanket order records the drawdown — ordered-so-far against committed. Not just the quantity copies, and the delivery date is per-order business, not the blanket's.

Reading the commitment: "how much of the 10,000 remains?" is read from the blanket order itself — its ordered-vs-committed quantities — not from the customer's memory, the last invoice, or stock levels. Both sides see the same consumption truth, which is precisely what makes volume agreements governable.

Blanket vs the alternatives: one giant 10,000-carton Sales Order reserves half a warehouse for months and lies about delivery intent. A quotation stretched to six-month validity is an offer awaiting an answer pretending to be an agreement being consumed — wrong document, wrong semantics. A pricing rule gives the rate but tracks no commitment. The blanket order is the instrument built for exactly this shape of deal — your Montaigne-class volume agreements belong here.

lessons.title: Sales Person — the internal team
lessons.html:
Sales Person models YOUR OWN sales force — and models it as a tree, not a flat list: Sales Director → Regional Managers → Field Reps. The tree is the point: results roll up the hierarchy, so the Lagos region's number is the sum of its reps' numbers and the director's number is the company, without anyone building spreadsheets.

Assignment on transactions: selling documents carry a Sales Team section where one or MORE sales persons are attached, each with a contribution % — and the percentages sum to 100. A deal worked by two reps splits 60/40: reports then credit each with their contributed share of the revenue, never double-counting the deal. Not two invoices for one sale, not a note in remarks, not two "sales partners" (wrong concept entirely — next lesson).

Targets: each sales person can carry targets by item group and period (monthly, quarterly). Actuals accrue from their assigned transactions.

The report: Sales Person-wise Transaction Summary — each person's transactions, contributed amounts, and performance against target. League tables, commission calculations, and performance conversations all read from here.

The consultant's honest answer — when a client asks "can we see sales by rep?": only if sales persons are assigned on the transactions. The report is arithmetic over assignments; installing it changes nothing, targets alone measure nothing, partners are a different object. The discipline of assignment precedes the report — configure the tree, make the Sales Team section mandatory in the client's process, and THEN the question answers itself weekly.

lessons.title: Sales Partner — the external channel
lessons.html:
A Sales Partner is a business OUTSIDE your company that brings you deals — a reseller, a referral agent, a channel distributor, an implementation partner who sources clients. The record carries the partner's identity, type, and — the operative field — a commission rate.

On transactions: select the Sales Partner on a Sales Order or Sales Invoice and two things happen: the deal is stamped as that channel's business (channel revenue becomes reportable), and the document computes the total commission at the partner's rate — the liability you owe them for the introduction, calculated per deal, automatically.

The distinction to keep razor-sharp — Person vs Partner:

  • Sales Person = internal staff: a tree, contribution percentages summing to 100, targets, performance management.
  • Sales Partner = an external business: a flat entity, a commission %, a payable relationship.

They are not the same thing with different names, commission is not what separates them (both can drive earnings), and a partner is not a customer. And a single transaction can legitimately carry BOTH: your rep (Sales Person, 100% contribution) worked a deal that a referral firm (Sales Partner, 5% commission) introduced.

Paying partners: commissions are settled from the Sales Partner-wise Transaction Summary — the system's own totals of each channel's business and accrued commission. Pay partners from the report, not from their claims: when the partner's invoice says ₦2.4m and your summary says ₦2.1m, the summary — built from the actual stamped transactions — is the negotiating position. Channel programs die of over-payment and under-tracking; this report prevents both.
